html:
SMTO-GWT-0066 — This GPU's speed settings can't be changed through SMTO

GUID: ea88f29f-d73a-5b2a-8773-81431c6c6ff2
Slug: gpu-clock-control-unsupported
Domain: GWT · Subsystem: gpu

What happened

  • Locking or resetting this graphics card's clock speed (how fast its processor or memory runs) isn't supported on this card, driver or computer. Nothing was changed.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. In the conversation, ask SMTO to show the clock capabilities for this GPU. It shows whether processor and memory speed changes are supported, and which speeds the card offers.
  2. If only one kind is unsupported, ask SMTO to change the other one instead (processor clock or memory clock). SMTO checks the two separately; some cards, such as NVIDIA Hopper models, allow processor clock changes but not memory clock changes.
  3. If you expected this to work, ask the person who manages the GPU computer to confirm it runs Linux with a current NVIDIA driver. SMTO only offers clock control on Linux, on recent NVIDIA card families, when the installed NVIDIA tools include the clock options.

What success looks like

  • The clock capabilities show the setting as supported, and SMTO reports that the card accepted the change.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages the computer with the GPU. Don't repeat the same request on this card; it will be refused the same way.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • GPU or memory clock control is unavailable: the capability check (Linux Gateway, Volta-or-newer architecture, reported supported clock pairs, lock/reset clock flags in nvidia-smi help; memory clocks not on Hopper) failed, or the provider rejected the clock operation as unsupported.

What this means

  • The current device profile lacked the requested GPU or memory clock-control capability, or the provider rejected that clock operation as unsupported. The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.

Why this can happen

  • The current device profile lacked the requested GPU or memory clock-control capability, or the provider rejected that clock operation as unsupported.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the specific GPU-versus-memory clock capability and driver response for the exact UUID.

How to fix it

  • Run gpu.clock_capabilities for the UUID and inspect gpu_clocks, memory_clocks and clocks.supported_pairs. Clock control requires a Linux Gateway, a Volta-or-newer GPU and an nvidia-smi that lists --lock-gpu-clocks/--reset-gpu-clocks (or the memory equivalents, which Hopper does not support); update the NVIDIA driver if the flags are missing.
  • Inspect gpu.clock_capabilities and the installed NVIDIA documentation.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect gpu.clock_capabilities and the installed NVIDIA documentation.

How to verify the fix

  • The requested operation is supported, with provider acknowledgment and documented clock-verification limits retained.

What not to do

  • Do not replay uncertain mutations, kill GPU clients automatically or invent sensor values.

Technical notes

  • The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
